nameStory: The sourwood gets its name from the distinctly sour, acidic taste of its leaves when chewed - they have a sharp, lemony tang that puckers your mouth! Early settlers and Native Americans knew this tree well, often calling it the 'sorrel tree' because its leaves taste similar to wood sorrel, another sour-leafed plant. The scientific name Oxydendrum literally means 'sour tree' in Greek.
description: Sourwood is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 20-30 feet tall in New England, though it can reach 50 feet in ideal southern conditions. It has a narrow, upright crown with slender branches that often droop slightly at the tips. The tree is most famous for its spectacular fall color - brilliant scarlet and orange leaves that seem to glow in autumn sunlight. In summer, it produces drooping clusters of small, white, bell-shaped flowers that look like tiny lily-of-the-valley blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Alternate, simple leaves that are 4-8 inches long with a distinctive sour taste when chewed. They're glossy dark green with fine teeth along the edges and prominent veins. Touch one - it feels smooth and somewhat thick, almost leathery.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Drooping, one-sided clusters of small white bell-shaped flowers appear in midsummer. Each tiny flower is about 1/4 inch long and looks like a miniature lily-of-the-valley bloom. The clusters can be 4-10 inches long and have a sweet, honey-like fragrance.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that develops deep furrows and scaly ridges on mature trees. Young trees have smoother bark with a reddish tinge. Run your hand along it - it feels rough and deeply textured on older specimens.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The seed capsules persist through winter, hanging in brown clusters that rattle when shaken by wind.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Narrow, upright tree with a distinctive silhouette - the branches tend to droop at the tips, giving it a slightly weeping appearance. Often leans or grows at an angle on slopes.

habitat: In New England, sourwood is quite rare and typically found in acidic, well-drained soils on rocky slopes and ridges, especially in oak-heath forests. Look for it in the southern parts of New England, particularly in Connecticut and western Massachusetts, often growing alongside mountain laurel, blueberries, and various oaks. It prefers partial shade and is most common at elevations below 2,000 feet.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge reddish-bronze before turning green. Look for the distinctive leaf shape and try the sour taste test on young foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with drooping white flower clusters in July and August. The sweet-scented blooms are unmistakable and attract many bees.
seasonality.fall: Spectacular scarlet to orange fall color appears early, often by late August. The brilliant leaves make it easily spotted from a distance.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic drooping habit, and brown seed clusters persist. The furrowed bark and narrow crown help with identification.

funFact: Sourwood honey is considered one of the finest honeys in the world, with a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor that's prized by gourmet chefs - but you'll have to travel south to Appalachia to taste it, since sourwood is too rare in New England to support commercial honey production!
confusionNotes: The drooping white flower clusters might remind you of Japanese pieris, but sourwood is a full-sized tree while pieris is a shrub, and sourwood's leaves have that distinctive sour taste. The narrow growth habit could be confused with black cherry, but cherry bark is very different and cherry leaves lack the sour taste.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with wood sorrel or sheep sorrel - those are completely different plants that just happen to share the sour taste! Sourwood is the only species in its genus worldwide, making it quite unique. It's much more common in the southern Appalachians, so finding one in New England is a real treat.
compareHints: Since sourwood is the only species in its genus, compare it to other heath family members like mountain laurel and rhododendrons. Unlike these shrubs, sourwood grows as a full tree and has alternate leaves rather than clustered evergreen leaves. Its drooping flower clusters and sour-tasting leaves make it unique among New England's heath family plants.
